entry.text: A shopfront on the square, swept clean, with a sign reading INTRODUCTIONS — DISCRETION — SUCCESS RATE 100%. Inside, behind a desk, a small brisk woman with a ledger and reading glasses is interviewing a nervous young man about his prospects. There is a waiting room. There are refreshments. There is a wall of framed portraits of happy couples going back sixty years, hundreds of them, and every single frame is hung perfectly level, and every single couple is photographed from a slight distance.

choices.label: Sit down and let her interview you
Wait until she is out and read the ledger

the_office.text: Matchmaking is the best-paid trade in the settlement and the office shows it: a strongbox of fees in scrap, a pantry of gift stock — preserves, good soap, bottled spirit — a medicine cabinet better than the clinic's, and a cellar door behind the desk with a very good lock on it. The ledger is immaculate. Two columns, names on the left, names on the right, ruled lines, dates, and every single line paired off and ticked. Six hundred and eleven matches. No failures. And on close reading, no line ever appears twice — nobody in this town has ever been matched, widowed, and matched again, which for sixty years of wasteland is not a statistic, it is a confession.

choices.label: Ask what is behind the cellar door
Take the key off the desk and open it yourself

the_cellar.text: The thing in the cellar has been under this square since before the settlement was a settlement, and it requires two, and it requires them willing, and it does not care about anything else. Sixty years ago a woman with a good head for records worked out that a town which supplies two willing people a year is a town that is otherwise left entirely alone — no raids, no sickness, no bad winters, none of it, the cellar sees to that — and she has run the cleanest, kindest, most scrupulously matched introductions service in the region ever since. Six hundred and eleven matches. Every one of them genuinely well-suited. Every one of them, she will tell you with real professional pride, happy. She is not a monster. She is a woman who has spent sixty years making sure that the two people who go down those stairs each year go down holding hands. She offers you the fee book, the gift pantry and the strongbox, and asks, without any threat in it at all, whether you happen to be travelling with anyone.

the_interview.text: She interviews you properly, which means an hour of questions of escalating precision, and by the end of it she knows your height, your reach, your appetite, your sleep, what you are frightened of and what you would do to keep it away from you — and she writes it all in the left-hand column, and you understand only afterward that nothing she asked had anything to do with romance.

the_waiting_room.text: The waiting room refreshments are excellent and the tea is on the house and about ten minutes after the tea your legs stop returning messages. You come round on the floor with the ledger still open at the page you were reading and a small brisk woman apologising for the inconvenience and helping you up.

she_is_honest.text: You ask, and she tells you, all of it, in order, without a flicker — and then she asks you, perfectly reasonably, what you would have done instead, and waits for an answer, and you do not have one, and the not having one costs you something you do not get back.

the_stairs.text: The cellar stairs are clean and swept and lit, because everything she runs is clean and swept and lit, and eleven steps down the thing at the bottom raises its attention to the door and finds one person standing in it. One is wrong. One is not what the arrangement says. It objects to the shortfall in the only way it has, and you come back up the stairs considerably faster than you went down and considerably less of you arrives at the top.
